claim: The lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) is thought to bind sensory events with the environment where they took place.
source: The lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) is thought to bind sensory events with the environment where they took place.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general understanding of LEC function, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Firing rates of some neurons were phasically selective for conditioned stimuli in a way that depended on which room the rat was in.
source: Firing rates of some neurons were phasically selective for conditioned stimuli in a way that depended on which room the rat was in
evidence: This is a primary finding from the neural recordings presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Nearly all neurons were tonically selective for environments in a way that depended on which stimuli had been presented in those environments.
source: nearly all neurons were tonically selective for environments in a way that depended on which stimuli had been presented in those environments.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the neural recordings, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: As rats moved from one environment to another, tonic neuron ensemble activity exhibited prospective information about the conditioned stimulus associated with the environment.
source: As rats moved from one environment to another, tonic neuron ensemble activity exhibited prospective information about the conditioned stimulus associated with the environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from ensemble analysis, supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: The LEC formed phasic and tonic codes for event-environment associations, thereby accurately differentiating multiple experiences with overlapping features.
source: Thus, the LEC formed phasic and tonic codes for event-environment associations, thereby accurately differentiating multiple experiences with overlapping features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The entorhinal cortex is thought to support rapid encoding of daily experiences by serving as an interface between the hippocampus and neocortical regions.
source: The entorhinal cortex is thought to support rapid encoding of daily experiences by serving as an interface between the hippocampus and neocortical regions (Eichenbaum, 2000; Squire, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lateral portions of the entorhinal cortex encode non-spatial information, such as objects.
source: In particular, lateral portions of the entorhinal cortex encode non-spatial information, such as objects (Deshmukh et al., 2012; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Keene et al., 2016; Tsao et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Lateral portions of the entorhinal cortex encode visual and olfactory stimuli.
source: lateral portions of the entorhinal cortex encode non-spatial information, such as objects (Deshmukh et al., 2012; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Keene et al., 2016; Tsao et al., 2013) as well as visual and olfactory stimuli (Igarashi et al., 2014; Leitner et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 1997; Xu and Wilson, 2012; Young et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Some cells in the LEC encode the location at which a specific object is placed.
source: For example, some cells in the LEC encode the location at which a specific object is placed (Keene et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Some cells in the LEC fire at the location of a previously encountered object or rewarding stimulus that is no longer present in the environment.
source: whereas other cells fire at the location of a previously encountered object or rewarding stimulus that is no longer present in the environment (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The LEC plays a role in recognizing objects in a specific context.
source: These findings are consistent with the LEC's role in recognizing objects in a specific context (Hunsaker et al., 2013; Van Cauter et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The LEC may encode the content of events with the environmental context in which they take place.
source: and suggest that the LEC may encode the content of events with the environmental context in which they take place.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: The acquisition and retrieval of trace eyeblink conditioning memory are known to depend on the LEC.
source: This paradigm was chosen because the acquisition and retrieval of memory are known to depend on the LEC (Morrissey et al., 2012; Ryou et al., 2001; Tanninen et al., 2013, 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Seven male Long-Evans rats weighing 500–600 g at the time of surgery were used in the experiment.
source: Seven male Long-Evans rats (Charles River Laboratories, St. Constant, QC, Canada) weighing 500–600 g at the time of surgery were used in the experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental subjects.

claim: The rats gradually increased the expression of CRs in the CS-US paired trials but not CS-alone trials.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Morrissey et al., 2017; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008), the rats gradually increased the expression of CRs in the CS-US paired trials but not CS-alone trials (Figure 1D; Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, Session × Block, F75, 450 = 2.99, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1D.

claim: The asymptotic level of CR expression during the three CS-US blocks was significantly different from that during the three CS-alone blocks.
source: The asymptotic level of CR expression during the three CS-US blocks was significantly different from that during the three CS-alone blocks (follow-up one-way repeated measures ANOVA on CR% during the last session, F5, 30 = 21.9, p<0.001, planned pairwise comparisons, ps < 0.05/6)
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The asymptotic level of CR expression was comparable between all three CS-US blocks.
source: but it was comparable between all three CS-US blocks (all ps > 0.7).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The increased frequency of eyeblink responses was not observed during the ITIs of any of six trial blocks.
source: In addition, the increased frequency of eyeblink responses was not observed during the ITIs of any of six trial blocks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Session × Block interaction, F70, 420 = 8.48, p=0.717)
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The eyeblink responses were conditioned to the CS, but not to the conditioning environment.
source: suggesting that the eyeblink responses were conditioned to the CS, but not to the conditioning environment (see also, Morrissey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data, also supported by a citation.

claim: In the last session, the frequency of CR expression changed upon the transition from the CS-alone to the CS-US block within the first ten trials.
source: In the last session, the frequency of CR expression changed upon the transition from the CS-alone to the CS-US block within the first ten trials (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by Figure 1E.

claim: Blocks of CS-alone trials did not simply extinguish associations acquired on previous days, rather they formed a distinct temporal context between earlier and later trials.
source: suggesting that blocks of CS-alone trials did not simply extinguish associations acquired on previous days, rather they formed a distinct temporal context between earlier and later trials.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: All except one rat responded correctly on the first trial of two blocks in which the change in stimulus contingency was signaled by the change in the conditioning environment.
source: On a trial-by-trial basis, all except one rat responded correctly on the first trial of two blocks in which the change in stimulus contingency was signaled by the change in the conditioning environment (Figure 1F, the performance of Rat 2, Figure 1G, the performance of four rats that underwent the trial blocks in the same temporal order).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: When the stimulus contingency was changed in the same environment, the rats gradually adjusted the frequency of CR expression over ten CS-US paired trials.
source: In contrast, when the stimulus contingency was changed in the same environment, the rats gradually adjusted the frequency of CR expression over ten CS-US paired trials
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the data.

claim: The presence of the US served as a cue for the block transition when stimulus contingency changed in the same environment.
source: suggesting that the presence of the US served as a cue for the block transition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: The rats formed three associative memories that shared a common, relational feature (the CS-US association) but differed in a discrete, physical feature (the sensory modality of the CS) or environmental context (Box 1 or 2).
source: Thus, the rats formed three associative memories that shared a common, relational feature (the CS-US association) but differed in a discrete, physical feature (the sensory modality of the CS) or environmental context (Box 1 or 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: The rats learned to use the change in conditioning environment and the presence of the US to rapidly infer whether the CS would be paired with the US in the current block.
source: They also learned to use the change in conditioning environment and the presence of the US to rapidly infer whether the CS would be paired with the US in the current block.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: 250 cells were recorded across seven rats.
source: Among 250 cells recorded across seven rats (Table 2)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data collection, supported by Table 2.

claim: 113 cells (45.2%) significantly changed their firing rate during the CS and subsequent intervals between CS offset and US onset relative to inter-trial intervals in at least one of six trial blocks.
source: 113 cells (45.2%) significantly changed their firing rate during the CS and subsequent intervals between CS offset and US onset relative to inter-trial intervals in at least one of six trial blocks (a random permutation test, α = 0.05; Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by statistical testing and Table 3.

claim: Of CS-responding cells, 8.8% showed selectivity for CS modality.
source: Of these CS-responding cells, 8.8% showed selectivity for CS modality, meaning that firing rates differed between the auditory CS and visual CS trials in Box 1, regardless of whether it was a CS-alone or CS-US paired trial (a random permutation test, α = 0.05; Figure 3A, Cell 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by statistical testing and Figure 3A.

claim: 6.2% of CS-responding cells were selective for the conditioning environment.
source: In parallel, a separate set of CS-responding cells, 6.2%, was selective for the conditioning environment, exhibiting significantly different firing rates between the auditory CS presented in Box 1 and that in Box 2, regardless of whether it was presented with the US or alone (Cell 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: 12.4% of CS-responding cells differentially responded to the CS depending on both CS modality and conditioning environment.
source: More cells (12.4%) differentially responded to the CS depending on both CS modality and conditioning environment (Cell 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: 9.7% of CS-responding cells differentiated the firing response to the CS depending on whether it was presented alone or paired with the US at least in one of six trial blocks.
source: In parallel, 9.7% differentiated the firing response to the CS depending on whether it was presented alone or paired with the US at least in one of six trial blocks (Relationship, Cell 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: The majority of CS-responding cells were selective for more than one task variable.
source: Overall, the majority of CS-responding cells were selective for more than one task variable (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: The proportion of cells in each selectivity category was comparable between superficial and deep layers of the LEC.
source: The proportion of cells in each selectivity category was comparable between superficial and deep layers of the LEC (Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Table 3.

claim: The magnitude of firing differentiation was similar between stimulus modality and conditioning environment.
source: The magnitude of firing differentiation as measured by the distribution of a shuffle-corrected 'Differential index' (below 0-no significant to 1-strongest differentiation), was similar between stimulus modality and conditioning environment (Figure 3C, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p=0.330)
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by statistical testing and Figure 3C.

claim: The magnitude of firing differentiation for stimulus relationship appeared to be weaker than those for modality and environment.
source: while the magnitude of firing differentiation for stimulus relationship appeared to be weaker than those for modality (p=0.103) and environment (p=0.016).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: A sizable proportion of LEC cells transiently signaled the stimulus-environment conjunction time-locked upon the CS presentation.
source: These results suggest that a sizable proportion of LEC cells transiently signaled the stimulus-environment conjunction time-locked upon the CS presentation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data analysis.

claim: Most cells (137, or 54.8%) did not significantly change firing rates upon the onset of the CS relative to inter-trial intervals.
source: Most cells (137, or 54.8%) did not significantly change firing rates upon the onset of the CS relative to inter-trial intervals (ITI).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: Nearly all non-CS-responding cells (97.9%) changed ITI firing rates depending on which trial block a rat was in.
source: These cells maintained stable firing rates throughout the entire period of each trial block, but nearly all of these cells (97.9%) changed ITI firing rates depending on which trial block a rat was in (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Virtually no cells (0.7%) were purely selective for conditioning environment.
source: Virtually no cells (0.7%) were purely selective for conditioning environment: the cells generally did not exhibit significantly different firing rates in Box 1 blocks compared with Box 2, independent of ACS-US pairings or ACS alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: A subset of non-responding cells, 9.2%, was selective for both environment and stimulus relationship.
source: Rather, a subset of non-responding cells, 9.2%, was selective for both environment and stimulus relationship, exhibiting differential firing rates for the ACS-US block compared with the ACS-alone block in only one of the conditioning boxes (Cell 8, relationship and environment).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: 25.9% of non-responding cells changed their ITI firing rates within the same conditioning environment depending on which of two CS was presented and whether the CS was paired with the US in a present trial block.
source: Furthermore, a separate set of cells (25.9%) changed their ITI firing rates within the same conditioning environment depending on which of two CS was presented and whether the CS was paired with the US in a present trial block (Cell 9, relationship and modality).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: The largest proportion of non-responding cells (38.9%) was classified as selective for the stimulus relationship, stimulus modality, and conditioning environment.
source: The largest proportion of cells (38.9%) was classified as selective for the stimulus relationship, stimulus modality, and conditioning environment, resulting in unique firing rates for one of six trial blocks (Cell 10) or different firing rates for each of six trial blocks (Cell 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: The substantial changes in ITI firing rates across the trial blocks were not due to instability of the recording.
source: Importantly, their spike waveforms were comparable between six trial blocks (bottom of each panel), suggesting that the substantial changes in ITI firing rates across the trial blocks were not due to instability of the recording (e.g., electrode drift).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistency of spike waveforms across trial blocks.

claim: Regardless of firing rate changes during events, nearly all cells in the LEC signaled highly integrated information about sensory events taking place in a given environment during intervals between the events.
source: These findings suggest that regardless of firing rate changes during events, nearly all cells in the LEC signaled highly integrated information about sensory events taking place in a given environment during intervals between the events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data analysis.

claim: Firing rates of the majority of cells were less than 2 Hz.
source: Firing rates of the majority of cells were less than 2 Hz (Figure 2C), which is consistent with those reported in the previous studies (Deshmukh et al., 2012; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 2C and citations to prior research.

claim: The majority of cells (96.4%) showed a smaller degree of firing fluctuation within each trial block than across the trial blocks.
source: The majority of cells (96.4%) showed a smaller degree of firing fluctuation, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence, within each trial block than across the trial blocks (Figure 5A right, B).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: As a population, the degree of within-block fluctuation was significantly smaller than that of the between-block fluctuation.
source: As a population, the degree of within-block fluctuation was significantly smaller than that of the between-block fluctuation (Figure 5C, signed rank test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by statistical testing and Figure 5C.

claim: The proportion of selective cells decreased as the bin size became shorter.
source: By re-running the test across multiple bin sizes, we found that the proportion of selective cells decreased as the bin size became shorter (Figure 5D), most likely due to the reduced accuracy in estimating firing rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: The proportion of selective cells and the type of selectivity was stable across the time bins regardless of their temporal proximity to the CS onset.
source: Importantly, the proportion of selective cells and the type of selectivity was stable across the time bins regardless of their temporal proximity to the CS onset (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: Firing rates of individual cells were largely homogeneous during the ITI period in a trial block.
source: These results suggest that firing rates of individual cells were largely homogeneous during the ITI period in a trial block.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data analysis.

claim: 5.7–7.9% of cells' firing rates during CS-US intervals were judged to be selective for CR expression.
source: Across three blocks of CS-US pairings, 5.7–7.9% of cells' firing rates during CS-US intervals were judged to be selective for CR expression (2 out of 35 cells in ACS-US in Box 1; 4 out of 61 cells in ACS-US in Box 2; 5 out of 63 cells in VCS-US in Box 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: Virtually no firing rates during the ITI period were selective for CR expression.
source: Virtually no firing rates during the ITI period were selective for CR expression (2 out of 35 cells in ACS-US in Box 1; 1 out of 61 cells in ACS-US in Box 2; 1 out of 63 cells in VCS-US in Box 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: Although the LEC is necessary for memory acquisition and expression of this associative learning paradigm, firing patterns of individual cells were not correlated with behavioral expression of the memory on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: These results suggest that although the LEC is necessary for memory acquisition and expression of this associative learning paradigm (Morrissey et al., 2012; Tanninen et al., 2015), firing patterns of individual cells were not correlated with behavioral expression of the memory on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data analysis, with citations to prior research establishing LEC's necessity.

claim: During trials, ensemble firing patterns differentiated between ACS and VCS trials (Modality), between CS-alone trials and CS-US trials (Relationship), and ACS trials in Box 1 and 2 (Environment) more strongly than odd- and even-numbered trials of the same block.
source: During trials, ensemble firing patterns differentiated between ACS and VCS trials (Modality), between CS-alone trials and CS-US trials (Relationship), and ACS trials in Box 1 and 2 (Environment) more strongly than odd- and even-numbered trials of the same block (None, the upper limit; n = 20 randomly selected sets of 10 trials per trial block; one-way ANOVA, F4, 195 = 238.975, p<0.001; posthoc test Tukey HSD, all ps < 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: The degree of differentiation was the strongest for stimulus modality.
source: The degree of differentiation was the strongest for stimulus modality (vs. Environment, p<0.001; vs. Relationship, p<0.001) and was comparable to the differentiation of two trial blocks without any overlapping variables (All, the lower limit, p=0.122).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: The differentiation of Relationship was weaker than the differentiation of Environment during trials.
source: Also, the differentiation of Relationship was weaker than the differentiation of Environment (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: During the ITI period, ensemble firing patterns differentiated two blocks with different stimulus modality more than those in different environments.
source: During the ITI period, ensemble firing patterns differentiated two blocks with different stimulus modality more than those in different environments (one-way ANOVA, F4, 195 = 142.092, p<0.001; posthoc Tukey HSD, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: The differentiation for stimulus relationship was significantly weaker than that for stimulus modality and conditioning environment but was stronger than the chance-level differentiation during ITI.
source: The differentiation for stimulus relationship was significantly weaker than that for stimulus modality (p<0.001) and conditioning environment (p<0.001) but was stronger than the chance-level differentiation (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: LEC formed ensemble codes that differentiated the six trial blocks not only during the trials but also during extended intervals between the trials.
source: Collectively, the analyses with two independent measures of ensemble selectivity suggest that LEC formed ensemble codes that differentiated the six trial blocks not only during the trials but also during extended intervals between the trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Ensemble firing in an ITI was similar to those in the other ITIs within the same trial block, though the similarity appeared to monotonically decrease across ITIs within each trial block.
source: Ensemble firing in an ITI was similar to those in the other ITIs within the same trial block, though the similarity appeared to monotonically decrease across ITIs within each trial block.
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Ensemble firing showed an abrupt transition after the shift from the ACS-US block in Box 1 to the ACS-alone block in Box 2.
source: In contrast to the gradual changes, ensemble firing showed an abrupt transition after the shift from the ACS-US block in Box 1 to the ACS-alone block in Box 2, (Figure 7B, template = the 70th trial) as well as the shift from the ACS-US block in Box 2 to the VCS alone block in Box 1 (template = the 140th trial).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: Block shifts involving the move from one box to the other resulted in a greater change in the ensemble firing than their spontaneous change within each block.
source: These block shifts involving the move from one box to the other resulted in a greater change in the ensemble firing (measured by a 'Similarity Score', 1- no change, 0-uncorrelated) than their spontaneous change within each block (Figure 7C, n = 20 runs with randomly sampled 100 neurons; t-test with Bonferroni corrections, ps <0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing and Figure 7C.

claim: The block shift involving the change in CS modality and conditioning environment induced a greater change in ensemble firing than the block shift involving the environmental change alone.
source: Notably, the block shift involving the change in CS modality and conditioning environment induced a greater change in ensemble firing than the block shift involving the environmental change alone (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: Over nine blocks of five sessions, the degree of ensemble transition upon the block shift with the environmental and modality change was increased.
source: Linear regression analyses showed that over nine blocks of five sessions, the degree of ensemble transition upon the block shift with the environmental and modality change was increased (Figure 7D, R2 = 0.944, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing and Figure 7D.

claim: Over nine blocks of five sessions, the degree of transition upon the block shift with the environmental change alone was decreased.
source: while the degree of transition upon the block shift with the environmental change alone was decreased (R2 = 0.508, p=0.031).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by statistical testing.

claim: The transition of ensemble activity preceded the first presentation of the CS upon the block shifts involving the environmental change, but not the block shifts involving the contingency change within the same environment.
source: These results suggest that the transition of ensemble activity preceded the first presentation of the CS upon the block shifts involving the environmental change, but not the block shifts involving the contingency change within the same environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Over two weeks of repeated exposures to the fixed temporal structure, the LEC ensembles gradually developed a greater sensitivity to the modality of the CS to be presented in the environment.
source: And, in the former case, over two weeks of repeated exposures to the fixed temporal structure, the LEC ensembles gradually developed a greater sensitivity to the modality of the CS to be presented in the environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ensemble analysis.

claim: The LEC plays a critical role in associating events with the environments in which they take place.
source: Accumulating evidence from behavioral and electrophysiological studies show that the LEC plays a critical role in associating events with the environments in which they take place (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Hunsaker et al., 2013; Keene et al., 2016; Tsao et al., 2013; Van Cauter et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cells in the LEC signaled event-environment conjunction not only during events ('phasic' coding) but also stably during extended periods between those events ('tonic' coding).
source: We show here that cells in the LEC signaled this event-environment conjunction not only during events ('phasic' coding) but also stably during extended periods between those events ('tonic' coding).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: The LEC may signal not only what is happening but also what had happened previously in an environment.
source: These results suggest that the LEC may signal not only what is happening but also what had happened previously in an environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Temporally precise, transient stimuli offered methodological advantages for discriminating between stimulus-evoked and stimulus-independent responses.
source: Temporally precise, transient stimuli offered methodological advantages for discriminating between stimulus-evoked and stimulus-independent responses, thereby overcoming a limitation of many previous investigations which used physical objects to characterize neuron activity (Deshmukh et al., 2012; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Keene et al., 2016; Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological observation with citations to prior research.

claim: ~45% of cells responded to the CS, which falls within the range of selective cells for unimodal sensory stimuli (47–90%).
source: In the present data set, ~45% of cells responded to the CS, which falls within the range of selective cells for unimodal sensory stimuli (47–90%, Leitner et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 1997; Xu and Wilson, 2012; Young et al., 1997)
evidence: This is a finding from the data, compared with prior research via citations.

claim: The proportion of CS-responding cells is higher than that of cells selective for object location (~30%).
source: but higher than that of cells selective for object location (~30%, Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research via citations.

claim: Some cells differentially responded to the CS depending on whether the CS was predictive of a US.
source: Some of these cells differentially responded to the CS depending on whether the CS was predictive of a US.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: Cells that differentially responded to the CS based on US prediction were also selective for the modality of the CS and environment in which the CS was presented.
source: Notably, these cells were also selective for the modality of the CS and environment in which the CS was presented (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 3.

claim: The conjunctive selectivity results in a clear separation of neural responses to the CS across six trial blocks.
source: This conjunctive selectivity results in a clear separation of neural responses to the CS across six trial blocks (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: The cells carry both behaviorally relevant and incidental information about the CS.
source: suggesting that the cells carry both behaviorally relevant and incidental information about the CS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neural data analysis.

claim: Almost no cells in the LEC differentiated firing patterns depending on CR expression on a trial by trial basis.
source: In contrast to the strong selectivity for the stimulus and environmental features of the task, almost no cells in the LEC differentiated firing patterns depending on CR expression on a trial by trial basis.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: The LEC may not be involved in the generation of CRs per se.
source: This finding suggests that the LEC may not be involved in the generation of CRs per se.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between LEC firing and CR expression.

claim: The LEC may play a role in differentiating the CS depending on the current situation.
source: Rather the LEC may play a role in differentiating the CS depending on the current situation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neural data analysis.

claim: Ensembles were strongly selective for the trial blocks that used visual compared with auditory CS.
source: Ensembles were strongly selective for the trial blocks that used visual compared with auditory CS, yet only about half of these cells changed firing rates at the time of CS presentations and maintained stable firing patterns throughout the entire period of a trial block.
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Virtually none of the cells were purely selective for the conditioning environment (independently from the stimulus features).
source: Notably, virtually none of these cells were purely selective for the conditioning environment (independently from the stimulus features), suggesting that they did not simply respond to perceivable differences between two conditioning boxes, such as patterns of the wall and lighting (see also Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, with a citation to related work.

claim: Differential firing rates were not reflective of variations of activity level across blocks.
source: Moreover, given the absence of a significant difference in spontaneous eyeblink activity across six trial blocks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), differential firing rates were not reflective of variations of activity level across blocks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A plausible interpretation is that these cells encode the conditioning environment with the history of sensory events that took place in that environment.
source: Therefore, a plausible interpretation would be that these cells encode the conditioning environment with the history of sensory events that took place in that environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural data.

claim: The hypothesis that differential activity patterns between task epochs were driven by past events in those same contexts is consistent with prior observations of neural activity patterns in the LEC.
source: The hypothesis that differential activity patterns between task epochs were driven by past events in those same contexts is consistent with prior observations of neural activity patterns in the LEC.
evidence: This is a statement connecting the current findings to prior research.

claim: Prior experience with an object can later evoke selective firing patterns in the LEC even after that object has been removed: an 'object-trace' code.
source: In particular, prior experience with an object can later evoke selective firing patterns in the LEC even after that object has been removed: an 'object-trace' code (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In previous studies, object-trace selectivity was observed in ~15% of LEC cells.
source: In these earlier studies, object-trace selectivity was observed in ~15% of LEC cells (Tsao et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The present results showed that virtually all cells in the LEC differentiated sensory stimuli that had been experienced tens of seconds or longer in the past.
source: while the present results showed that virtually all cells in the LEC differentiated sensory stimuli that had been experienced tens of seconds or longer in the past.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis.

claim: The difference in proportion of selective cells may be in part because the criteria for significance were based on the averaged firing rate across 9 s periods before CS presentations.
source: This difference may be in part because our criteria for significance were based on the averaged firing rate across 9 s periods before CS presentations.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation for differences with prior studies.

claim: The long time window serves as a kind of a 'low-pass-filter' that cancels out variations in spike timing across trials.
source: This long time window serves as a kind of a 'low-pass-filter' that cancels out variations in spike timing across trials.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation.

claim: The proportion of selective cells dropped down to ~50% when shorter bin sizes were used.
source: In fact, the proportion of selective cells dropped down to ~50% when shorter bin sizes were used (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the neural data analysis, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: The total number of repeated stimulus presentations is far greater than the repetition of object presentations used in previous studies.
source: The total number of repeated stimulus presentations, therefore, is far greater than the repetition of object presentations used in the previous studies (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison with prior studies via citations.

claim: The task design could have facilitated the development of an internal model of the stimulus, which may be reflected in the high proportion of cells that maintain the selectivity during the stimulus-free periods.
source: This task design could have facilitated the development of an internal model of the stimulus, which may be reflected in the high proportion of cells that maintain the selectivity during the stimulus-free periods.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Changes in ensemble activity during stimulus-free periods were tightly coupled with the shift of trial blocks with the change in the conditioning environment.
source: Notably, changes in ensemble activity during stimulus-free periods were tightly coupled with the shift of trial blocks with the change in the conditioning environment.
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis.

claim: When rats moved from one conditioning box to the other, ensemble activity showed abrupt transition before the first presentation of the CS.
source: When rats moved from one conditioning box to the other, ensemble activity showed abrupt transition before the first presentation of the CS (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by Figures 7A-C.

claim: Initially, the degree of ensemble transition was comparable regardless of whether the rats were to receive the different or same modality of the CS from/as the one in the previous block.
source: Initially, the degree of ensemble transition was comparable regardless of whether the rats were to receive the different or same modality of the CS from/as the one in the previous block.
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Over two weeks, the degree of ensemble transition became greater for the block shift with the different CS than the one with the same CS.
source: Over two weeks, however, it became greater for the block shift with the different CS than the one with the same CS (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: The LEC keeps track of what had happened in a given environment in the past and prospectively signals the information when the rat enters the environment next time.
source: This observation suggests that the LEC keeps track of what had happened in a given environment in the past and prospectively signals the information when the rat enters the environment next time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Some cells in the cortex change their responses to a sensory stimulus or environment over repetitive presentations.
source: In support of this view, some cells in the cortex change their responses to a sensory stimulus (Fahy et al., 1993; Riches et al., 1991; Suzuki et al., 1997) or environment (Takehara-Nishiuchi et al., 2013) over repetitive presentations of the stimulus
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cells may keep track of the temporal order or repetition of experiences.
source: suggesting that they may keep track of the temporal order or repetition of experiences.
evidence: This is an inference from prior research.

claim: Within each trial block, the similarity of ensemble firing between stimulus-free periods decreased with time.
source: In fact, within each trial block, the similarity of ensemble firing between stimulus-free periods decreased with time (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: The time-dependent change in the ensemble activity was substantially smaller than the changes upon the shift of two trial blocks in the different environment.
source: This time-dependent change in the ensemble activity, however, was substantially smaller than the changes upon the shift of two trial blocks in the different environment (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: Time alone is not sufficient to account for the observed across-block changes in ensemble firing.
source: suggesting that time alone is not sufficient to account for the observed across-block changes in ensemble firing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ensemble analysis.

claim: In general, ensemble selectivity was higher for stimulus modality (auditory vs. visual CS) compared with conditioning environment (Box 1 vs. 2).
source: In general, ensemble selectivity was higher for stimulus modality (auditory vs. visual CS) compared with conditioning environment (Box 1 vs. 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis.

claim: LEC ensembles show greater selectivity for object identity compared with object location.
source: This observation could be considered alongside previous observations that LEC ensembles show greater selectivity for object identity compared with object location (Keene et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The physical features of sensory events have a strong influence on the neuron activity in the LEC.
source: and suggests that the physical features of sensory events have a strong influence on the neuron activity in the LEC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ensemble analysis and comparison with prior research.

claim: The selectivity of LEC ensembles was weaker for stimulus relationship (CS-US paired vs. CS alone) than stimulus modality.
source: In parallel the selectivity of LEC ensembles was weaker for stimulus relationship (CS-US paired vs. CS alone) than stimulus modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the ensemble analysis.

claim: Stimulus relationship was a critical factor for adaptive behavior while stimulus modality and conditioning environment were not.
source: In our paradigm, stimulus relationship was a critical factor for adaptive behavior while stimulus modality and conditioning environment were not.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design.

claim: The stronger selectivity for behaviorally irrelevant over relevant features sharply contrasts with the opposite selectivity observed in neuron ensembles in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) during the same behavioral paradigm.
source: The stronger selectivity for behaviorally irrelevant over relevant features sharply contrasts with the opposite selectivity observed in neuron ensembles in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) during the same behavioral paradigm (Morrissey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research via citation.

claim: These findings indicate a difference in information organization between the LEC and mPFC, the LEC being more sensitive to incidental details of experiences and the mPFC being more sensitive to their behaviorally relevant features.
source: These findings indicate a difference in information organization between the two regions, the LEC being more sensitive to incidental details of experiences and the mPFC being more sensitive to their behaviorally relevant features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison with prior research.

claim: The difference in feature selectivity may underlie the complementary roles that the hippocampal system and prefrontal cortex play for memory formation, consolidation, and assimilation.
source: The difference in feature selectivity may underlie the complementary roles that the hippocampal system and prefrontal cortex play for memory formation, consolidation, and assimilation (Morrissey et al., 2017; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Memories of daily experiences are thought to reside in a hippocampal-rhinal-neocortical network within which information becomes increasingly well integrated as it flows from the neocortical associative areas to the hippocampus.
source: Memories of daily experiences are thought to reside in a hippocampal-rhinal-neocortical network within which information becomes increasingly well integrated as it flows from the neocortical associative areas to the hippocampus (Eichenbaum, 2000; Squire, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The presently observed selectivity of LEC cells suggests that the perceivable and relational information of experiences has already been highly integrated at the level of the LEC.
source: The presently observed selectivity of LEC cells suggests that the perceivable and relational information of experiences has already been highly integrated at the level of the LEC, even to a comparable level that was reported in the hippocampus (Komorowski et al., 2013; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Moita et al., 2003; Wood et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings, with citations to prior research on the hippocampus.

claim: The LEC may not differ from other regions regarding the level of information integration, but it may make a unique contribution to memory formation and retrieval by stably maintaining the highly integrated information throughout the experience.
source: The LEC, therefore, may not differ from the other regions regarding the level of information integration, but it may make a unique contribution to memory formation and retrieval by stably maintaining the highly integrated information throughout the experience.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Such representations may serve as a scaffold in which efferent regions, such as the hippocampus, embed temporal dynamics of events within an experience, thereby facilitating accurately encoding the content of each experience.
source: Such representations may serve as a scaffold in which efferent regions, such as the hippocampus, embed temporal dynamics of events within an experience, thereby facilitating accurately encoding the content of each experience.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: LEC representations may play a role in the retrieval of appropriate information based on the similarity between a present situation and situations encountered in the past.
source: They also play a role in the retrieval of appropriate information based on the similarity between a present situation and situations encountered in the past.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The present findings support an emerging view that all regions within the hippocampal system encode the highly integrated information of sensory and environmental features of an experience.
source: In summary, the present findings support an emerging view that all regions within the hippocampal system encode the highly integrated information of sensory and environmental features of an experience (Keene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings, with a citation to prior research.

claim: The LEC may be unique in that it signals the information not only during specific events but also stably throughout the experience.
source: The LEC may be unique in that it signals the information not only during specific events but also stably throughout the experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: This coding property may support the LEC's involvement in the accurate binding of physical, relational, and contextual features of everyday experiences.
source: This coding property may support the LEC's involvement in the accurate binding of physical, relational, and contextual features of everyday experiences (Eichenbaum, 2000; Morrissey and Takehara-Nishiuchi, 2014; Squire, 1992).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Toronto.
source: All surgical and experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Toronto.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The rats were maintained on a reversed 12 hr light-dark circadian cycle, and all experiments took place during the dark part of the cycle.
source: They were maintained on a reversed 12 hr light-dark circadian cycle, and all experiments took place during the dark part of the cycle.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: The final locations of the tetrodes were evenly distributed along the anterior-posterior axis within the LEC.
source: The final locations of the tetrodes were evenly distributed along the anterior-posterior axis within the LEC (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by Figures 2A and 2B.
